{{Short description|Statistical fallacy}}
The '''Texas sharpshooter fallacy''' is the [[statistical fallacy]] of inferring meaning from what is essentially a random distribution of data points. It is the philosophical or rhetorical application of the [[multiple comparisons]] problem (also known as [[data dredging]] or ''p''-hacking in statistics) and [[apophenia]] (in cognitive psychology). It is related to the [[clustering illusion]], which is the tendency in human [[cognition]] to interpret patterns where none actually exist, itself stemming from the tendency to underestimate the likelihood of clusters appearing in random or [[Pseudorandomness|pseudorandom]] datasets.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gilovich |first=Thomas |url=http://archive.org/details/howweknowwhatisn00gilorich |title=How we know what isn't so : the fallibility of human reason in everyday life |date=1991 |publisher=New York, N.Y. : Free Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-02-911705-7}}</ref>

The name comes from an anecdote about a person in [[Texas]] who fires a gun at the side of a barn, with bullets landing in a [[random distribution]]. He then paints a [[shooting target|target]] around the tightest [[Shot grouping|cluster]] of shots and claims to be a [[sharpshooter]].<ref name="Grufferman">{{cite journal |last=Grufferman |first=Seymour |date=1977 |title=Clustering and aggregation of exposures in Hodgkin's disease |journal=[[Cancer (journal)|Cancer]] |volume=38 |issue=54 |pages=1829–1833 |doi=10.1002/1097-0142(197704)39:4+<1829::aid-cncr2820390815>3.0.co;2-a |doi-access=free |issn=0008-543X}}</ref><ref name="gawande">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/hhsa/programs/phs/documents/PHS_Cancer_Concerns_Cancer_Cluster_Myth_Gawande99-NewYorker.pdf|title=The cancer-cluster myth|author=Atul Gawande|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|date=1999-08-02|access-date=2025-02-22}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last1 = Carroll | first1 = Robert Todd | author-link1 = Robert Todd Carroll | title = The Skeptic's Dictionary: a collection of strange beliefs, amusing deceptions, and dangerous delusions | publisher = John Wiley & Sons | year = 2003 | page = 375 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=6FPqDFx40vYC&q=texas+sharpshooter&pg=PA375 | access-date = 2012-03-25 | isbn = 0-471-27242-6 }}</ref>

== History ==
The mathematician [[John Venn]] presented the statistical fallacy and the shooting analogy in 1866:<ref name="origins">{{Cite web |last=Wagenmakers |first=Eric-Jan |date=2018-01-11 |title=Origin of the Texas Sharpshooter |url=https://www.bayesianspectacles.org/origin-of-the-texas-sharpshooter/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=Bayesian Spectacles |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{Blockquote|text=One of the most fertile sources of error and confusion... consists in choosing the class to which to refer an event, and therefore judging of the rarity of the event and the consequent improbability of foretelling it, after it has happened, and then transferring the impressions we experience to a supposed contemplation of the event beforehand.... No error therefore need arise in this way, if we were careful as to the class which we thus selected; but such carefulness is often neglected.
<p>An illustration may afford help here. A man once pointed to a small target chalked upon a door, the target having a bullet hole through the centre of it, and surprised some spectators by declaring that he had fired that shot from an old fowling-piece at a distance of a hundred yards. His statement was true enough, but he suppressed a rather important fact. The shot had really been aimed in a general way at the barn-door, and had hit it; the target was afterwards chalked round the spot where the bullet struck. A deception analogous to this is, I think, often practised unconsciously in other matters. We judge of events on a similar principle, feeling and expressing surprise in an equally unreasonable way, and deciding as to their occurrence on grounds which are really merely a subsequent adjunct of our own.</p>|author=John Venn|title=''The Logic of Chance''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Venn |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/logicchanceanes01venngoog/page/n291/mode/2up |title=The Logic Of Chance |date=1866 |publisher=Macmillan And Company. |others= |edition=1st |location=London and Cambridge |publication-date=1866 |pages=259 |language=en}}</ref>}}The story about drawing the target after making the shot is older than that. A version involving arrows is attributed to the [[Dubno maggid|Dubno Maggid]] (died 1804),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stansbury |first=Mark |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Irish_in_Early_Medieval_Europe/MyRIEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1 |title=The Irish in Early Medieval Europe: Identity, Culture and Religion |last2= |first2= |date=2017-09-16 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-137-43061-8 |editor-last=Flechner |editor-first=Roy |pages=123 |language=en |chapter=Irish Biblical Exegesis |editor-last2=Meeder |editor-first2=Sven}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rossel |first=Seymour |url=http://archive.org/details/isbn_9781602801714 |title=Essential Jewish Stories |date=2011 |publisher=KTAV |others= |isbn=978-1-60280-171-4 |pages=87-88 |language=en |via=Internet Archive}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wagenmakers |first=Eric-Jan |date=2024-07-14 |title=Origin of the Texas Sharpshooter II: The Dubner Maggid |url=https://www.bayesianspectacles.org/origin-of-the-texas-sharpshooter-ii-the-dubner-maggid/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=Bayesian Spectacles |language=en-US}}</ref> and similar stories are probably older.<ref name="origins" />

In the modern statistical literature, the story of a specifically ''Texas'' sharpshooter is first mentioned in 1977,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grufferman |first=Seymour |date=1977 |title=Clustering and aggregation of exposures in Hodgkin's disease |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/1097-0142%28197704%2939%3A4%20%3C1829%3A%3AAID-CNCR2820390815%3E3.0.CO%3B2-A |journal=Cancer |language=en |volume=39 |issue=S4 |pages=1830 |doi=10.1002/1097-0142(197704)39:4+<1829::AID-CNCR2820390815>3.0.CO;2-A |issn=1097-0142|url-access=subscription }}</ref> perhaps drawing on the stereotype of Texans as tellers of [[Tall tale|tall tales]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boatright |first=Mody Coggin |url=http://archive.org/details/talltalesfromtex00boat |title=Tall tales from Texas |date=1934 |publisher=Dallas, Tex. : The Southwest Press |others=The Library of Congress}}</ref> In the [[American Civil War]], there was in fact a 1st Battalion of Texas Sharpshooters, but there is no obvious connection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1st Battalion Texas Sharpshooters - Vicksburg National Military Park |url=https://www.nps.gov/vick/learn/historyculture/1st-battalion-texas-sharpshooters.htm |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=U.S. National Park Service |language=en}}</ref> The Texas sharpshooter was popularized by [[Atul Gawande]] in 1999.<ref name="gawande" />

== Structure ==
[[File:Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy illustration.png|thumb|A set of 100 randomly generated points displayed on a scatter graph. Examining the points, it is easy to identify apparent patterns. In particular, rather than spreading out evenly, it is not uncommon for random data points to form clusters, giving the (false) impression of "hot spots" created by some underlying cause.]]
The Texas sharpshooter fallacy often arises when a conclusion is based on the analysis of a highly restricted subset of available data. Some factor other than the one attributed may give all the elements in that subset some common property (or pair of common properties, when arguing for [[correlation]]). If the person attempts to account for the likelihood of finding ''some'' subset in the large data with ''some'' common property by a factor other than its actual cause, the person is likely committing a Texas sharpshooter fallacy.

The fallacy is characterized by the failure to specify a hypothesis before gathering data, or to formulate one only after data has been collected and reviewed ([[HARKing]]).<ref>{{cite journal | title = Painting the target around the matching profile: the Texas sharpshooter fallacy in forensic DNA interpretation | journal = Law, Probability, & Risk | date = July 18, 2009 | first = William C. | last = Thompson | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 257–258| url = http://lpr.oxfordjournals.org/content/8/3/257.full.pdf+html | access-date = 2012-03-25 | quote = Texas sharpshooter fallacy...this article demonstrates how post hoc target shifting occurs and how it can distort the frequency and likelihood ratio statistics used to characterize DNA matches, making matches appear more probative than they actually are. | doi=10.1093/lpr/mgp013| doi-access = free }}</ref> Thus, it typically does not apply if one had an ''[[ex ante]]'', or prior, expectation of the particular relationship in question before examining the data. For example, before examining the information, one might have in mind a specific physical mechanism implying the particular relationship. One could then use the information to give support or cast doubt on the presence of that mechanism. Alternatively, if a second set of additional information can be generated using the same process as the original information, one can use the first (original) set of information to construct a hypothesis, and then test the hypothesis on the second (new) set of information. (See [[hypothesis testing]].) However, after constructing a hypothesis on a set of data, one would be committing the Texas sharpshooter fallacy if they then tested that hypothesis on the same data (see [[hypotheses suggested by the data]]).{{cn|date=May 2026}}

== Examples ==

=== Epidemiology ===
The Texas Sharpshooter Effect is arguably most commonly seen in epidemiology.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goodman |first=Anna C. |date=2007-03-03 |title=Beware the "Texas sharp shooter" in rate ratios of progression |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1808165/ |journal=BMJ (Clinical research ed.) |volume=334 |issue=7591 |pages=440 |doi=10.1136/bmj.39136.475313.FA |issn=1756-1833 |pmc=1808165 |pmid=17332546}}</ref> In 1993, Swedish researchers reported the results of study designed to investigate whether long-term proximity to [[Overhead power line|high-voltage power lines]] was [[Electromagnetic radiation and health|linked to negative health outcomes]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Feychting |first1=M. |last2=Ahlbom |first2=A. |date=1993 |title=Magnetic fields and cancer in children residing near Swedish high-voltage power lines |journal=[[American Journal of Epidemiology]] |volume=138 |issue=7 |pages=467–481 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a116881 |issn=0002-9262 |pmid=8213751}}</ref> Health surveys of people living within 300 metres of such power lines were undertaken over a 25-year period, following which the data collected was analysed in order to determine whether a [[statistical significance|statistically significant]] increase could be detected in the prevalence of over 800 medical conditions, when compared to people who lived further away. The study found that the incidence of childhood [[leukemia]] was four times higher in the former group, prompting calls for action by the Swedish government.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Coghlan |first=Andy |date=31 October 1992 |title=Swedish studies pinpoint power line cancer link |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg13618450-300-swedish-studies-pinpoint-power-line-cancer-link/ |magazine=[[New Scientist]] |issue=1845}}</ref> The problem with the conclusion, however, was that the number of potential ailments, i.e., over 800, was so large that it created a high probability that at least one ailment would have a statistically significant correlation with living distance from power lines by chance alone, a situation known as the [[multiple comparisons problem]]. Subsequent studies failed to show any association between power lines and childhood leukemia.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/programs/transcripts/1319.html |title=Frontline: previous reports: transcripts: currents of fear |website=PBS |date=1995-06-13 |access-date=2012-07-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203040412/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/programs/transcripts/1319.html|archive-date=2016-02-03}}</ref> 

=== Pharmaceutical Drug Development ===
The fallacy routinely appears in the publication of data on drug efficacy,<ref>{{Cite web |last=McGinley |first=Laurie |title=Alzheimer's drug sparks emotional battle as FDA nears deadline on whether to approve |url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/life/wellness/2021/05/31/alzheimers-drug-sparks-emotional-battle-fda-nears-deadline-whether-approve-tdn/5284696001/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Detroit News |language=en-US}}</ref> and has been recognised as being built-into many tools of drug discovery and design.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Qin |first=Rui |last2=Chen |first2=Zijie |last3=Li |first3=Yurong |last4=Fang |first4=Meijing |last5=Shen |first5=Longji |last6=Su |first6=Yilong |last7=Zhang |first7=Odin |last8=Wang |first8=Qinghan |last9=Su |first9=Qun |last10=Wang |first10=Jike |last11=Hou |first11=Tingjun |last12=Kang |first12=Yu |title=Revisiting Target-Aware de novo Molecular Generation with TarPass: Between Rational Design and Texas Sharpshooter |url=https://chemrxiv.org/doi/full/10.26434/chemrxiv-2026-dhdqk |journal=ChemRxiv |volume=2026 |issue=0102 |doi=10.26434/chemrxiv-2026-dhdqk}}</ref> A drug may have no effect yet still produce a statistically significant effect in a specific subgroup if a sufficient number of analyses are run; the effect is not real, but is rather the result of a target being drawn around a cluster of random, positive data points. The effect will disappear when the test is replicated. 
[[File:Texas-discovery-machine.png|alt=texas sharpshooter fallacy|center|thumb|857x857px|A graph showing the Texas Sharpshooter fallacy in action. The drug is ineffective, but after repeated analyses a subgroup is identified with a "good enough" p-value, and is then marketed as effective for that subgroup. The effect is random noise, with a target drawn around it after the fact. Originally taken from Unspurious.com. ]]


For example, a drug with no effect might appear to be highly effective in twins, simply by virtue of the false positives clustering around that subgroup. The researcher did not set out to see if the drug was effective on twins. The target was drawn around the random cluster after the fact, suggesting a meaningful pattern in what is essentially a random distribution of results. If enough analyses are run on the data, some subgroup can always be identified which shows a strong response to the drug.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Texas sharpshooter fallacy — explained interactively |url=https://unspurious.com/texas-sharpshooter.html |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=unspurious |language=en}}</ref>

=== Predictions ===
The fallacy is often found in modern-day interpretations of the [[quatrain]]s of [[Nostradamus]].<ref name="Forshaw">{{cite book |last=Forshaw |first=Mark |date=2012 |title=Critical Thinking for Psychology: A Student Guide |location=London |publisher=BPS Blackwell |pages=49–51 |isbn=978-1405191180}}</ref> Nostradamus's quatrains are often liberally translated from their original [[Middle French]] versions, in which their historical context is often lost, and then applied to support the erroneous conclusion that Nostradamus predicted a given modern-day event after the event actually occurred.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.snopes.com/rumors/nostradamus.asp |title=Nostradamus Predicted 9/11? |website=snopes.com|date=12 September 2001 |access-date=2012-07-03}}</ref>
